analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from permanently replacing workers who go on strike.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 247-182, but the Senate never voted on it and it died when the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it an unfair labor practice for an employer to hire a permanent replacement for a worker who strikes through a union, or to favor a replacement worker over a striker who has offered to come back to work. It applied the same rule to airlines and railroads under the Railway Labor Act. It passed the House 247-182 in July 1991, but the Senate never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.who_benefits: Unionized workers who go on strike. Under the law at the time, employers could legally hire permanent replacements, which meant a striking worker risked losing their job for good — the strongest lever an employer had in a labor dispute. This bill would have removed that threat, protected strikers' jobs when they unconditionally offered to return, and extended the same protections to airline and railroad workers. Workers trying to form a union would also have gained protection once a representation petition was on file.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it an unfair labor practice for an employer to hire a permanent replacement for an employee who was in a union-represented bargaining unit, or a unit with a pending union representation petition, and who engaged in union-organized concerted activity during the dispute.

Bars employers from denying jobs or other employment rights to strikers who have unconditionally offered to return to work, out of preference for people who worked, or offered to work, during the dispute.
Applies the same prohibition on permanent replacements and replacement-based job preferences to airlines and railroads under the Railway Labor Act.

By taking permanent replacement off the table, the bill would have shifted bargaining leverage toward striking workers, whose main protection under existing law was the legal risk of losing their jobs permanently.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, chiefly unionized companies, airlines, and railroads. They would lose the ability to staff operations during a strike with permanent replacements and would have to hold strikers' jobs open, bearing the disruption and cost of longer work stoppages. Employers argued those costs would ultimately reach consumers through higher prices or lost service during strikes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers facing strikes, especially unionized firms

drawbacks.text: The bill removes an employer's main tool for keeping planes, trains, and plants running during a strike, which businesses and the Bush administration's Labor Department opposed — the Labor Department submitted unfavorable executive comment on the bill in March 1991.

The protection is narrower than it first appears: it covers only employees who were in a union-represented bargaining unit, or a unit with a pending representation petition filed at least 30 days before the dispute, and who acted through a labor organization — so workers acting outside a union, and workplaces with no union presence, get nothing.

Employers argued the ban would hand unions outsize leverage, inviting longer strikes and giving workers little incentive to settle, with the costs of prolonged stoppages landing on customers and employers alike.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is leverage in labor disputes: workers would gain the ability to strike without risking their jobs, while employers would lose the ability to run their businesses with permanent replacements during a stoppage. For unionized workers the benefit is substantial and direct — the permanent-replacement threat was the decisive weapon against strikes. The costs fall on a narrower set of employers during disputes, though those costs can be real and can spill over into prices and service. The bill's coverage limits (union units only) make it a targeted change, not a rewrite of labor law. On balance, the gains for workers outweigh the concentrated costs on employers, but the employer-side objections were not trivial.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 247-182 on July 17, 1991, but the Senate left it on its calendar without ever voting, and it died when that Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. William Clay introduced the bill on January 3, 1991, and it was referred to three House committees: Education and Labor, Energy and Commerce, and Public Works and Transportation.
All three committees amended and reported the bill between May and June 1991, and it was placed on the Union Calendar on June 27, 1991.
The House passed the bill on July 17, 1991, by a recorded vote of 247-182 — 230 of 267 Democrats in favor, 16 of 166 Republicans in favor.
The Senate received the bill the next day and placed it on its legislative calendar, where it sat with no floor action for the rest of the Congress.

Outside the record, Senate Republicans made clear they would not allow the ban to reach a vote — they filibustered the Senate's companion striker-replacement bill in 1992 — and President George H.W. Bush, whose Labor Department had opposed H.R. 5, vetoed that companion bill later the same year.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers — especially unionized companies, airlines, and railroads — kept the legal right to permanently replace strikers and gave up nothing. Striking workers remained at risk of losing their jobs permanently.

for.name: William (Bill) Clay
for.role: Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced H.R. 5 on January 3, 1991 and steered it through committee; his committee reported the bill on June 27, 1991.

for.name: George Mitchell
for.what_they_did: Supported the striker-replacement ban and pursued it through the Senate's companion bill in 1992 rather than bringing H.R. 5 itself off the calendar for a vote.

against.name: 149 of 166 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage; Rep. Goodling moved to recommit the bill to committee, and the motion failed by voice vote.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Refused to allow the ban to come to a Senate vote; H.R. 5 sat on the Senate calendar from July 1991 until the Congress ended, and Senate Republicans filibustered the companion striker-replacement bill to death in 1992.

against.name: George H.W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Opposed the ban; his Labor Department submitted unfavorable executive comment on H.R. 5 in March 1991, and he later vetoed the Senate companion bill.

sides.party_line_note: House Democrats backed the bill 230-33 while House Republicans opposed it 16-149; the bill cleared the House 247-182 but had almost no Republican support.

industries.industry: Unionized employers (manufacturing and service firms with union workforces)
industries.note: The bill would have taken away their ability to replace strikers permanently, forcing them to keep strikers' jobs open during disputes. Their savings from that practice came directly at striking workers' expense.

The bill amends the Railway Labor Act to bar carriers from granting permanent replacement status or replacement-based job preferences during labor disputes, removing their ability to keep running flights and trains with new permanent hires during a stoppage.

The ban would have made strikes far less risky for union members and strengthened unions' bargaining position, since employers could no longer credibly threaten to replace strikers for good. Workers gained leverage; unions gained the same.
